title: Stage boundaries and closing
blurb: Run a stage boundary around the release planning workshop and close a project through the right activities and closure workshop topics.
question: At the end of Draycott Precision Engineering's stage 2, the teams agree OKRs for Release 2 and break the next features into user stories. Which process and workshop is this, and how does it differ from the team planning workshop?

teach.h: Look back, look ahead, then let go
teach.body: Managing a stage boundary gives the board enough information to review the success of the current stage, review the updated release map, approve the next stage plan (the updated release map) and confirm that the business justification and risks are still acceptable. Closing a project provides a fixed point to confirm acceptance of the project product and hand it over. Closing happens inside the final stage; it is not a stage of its own.
teach.cite: PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 13.7.1, 13.8; PRINCE2 7 manual 19.1

tasks.label: Stage 4: Release 3 + closure
tasks.sub: Factory B; closing in the final stage

teach.caption: A release planning workshop is held for initiation (planning stage 2) and at each later boundary.

teach.body: At a stage boundary the PM, with the project team, reviews and if necessary updates the parts of the PID, reviews the lessons to apply to the next stage, and updates the release map with the details for the next stage. The board then approves that updated release map in 'authorize a stage or exception plan'. Planning stays high level: task planning is left to the teams, iteration by iteration.
teach.cite: PRINCE2 Agile V2 book Table 13.15, Table 13.4

head: Topic
What happens
rows: Present the canvas, project backlog and release map; gather feedback
Define or update team OKRs: aspirational objectives, measurable key results
Break key activities into user stories; update the release map
Review the key outputs of the workshop
teach.caption: 13.7.4.1 and Table 13.16. The PM defines participants, sets dates and invites them (13.7.3).

head: Activity
What the PM does
rows: Identify who must know; update the project log and release map with final actuals; draft the closure notification
Follow-on actions for unfinished work, issues and risks; check post-project benefits work; confirm hand-over to operations
Compare with the original PID and approved changes; end project report; lessons report
Brief the board on performance and readiness; note concessions for off-specifications
teach.caption: Table 13.18.

head: Topic
Goal
rows: Update PID, logs, project dashboard and Agilometer
Actionable lessons, with Agilometer and psychological safety trends
Support responsibilities, operational needs, benefits actions
teach.caption: 13.8.4 and Table 13.19. The workshop confirms the product, reflects on lessons, finalizes documentation and prepares the move to operations.

teach.h: From closing to the board's decision
teach.caption: In 'authorize project closure' the board compares the original and current PID, approves the end project report, ensures post-project benefits reviews and confirms the updated canvas (Table 13.4).

teach.h: Worked scenario: Draycott Precision Engineering's Smart Maintenance
teach.body: At the end of stage 2, Andrea Lucas updates the PID, applies lessons from fitting sensors and runs the release planning workshop. The teams agree an objective of trusted early warnings with a key result such as alerts on all Factory A machines, then break the work into stories on the release map. The board approves it. At month 12 the closure workshop demos the Factory B dashboard to Ruth Kenyon's engineers, records Agilometer trends in the lessons report and plans hand-over and benefits actions.

teach.text: Traps: the release planning workshop (stage boundary, release map, OKRs) is not the team planning workshop (next iteration, team plan). In the closure workshop, 'project lessons' presents what was gathered, while 'lessons report' turns it into actions for future projects; 'progress review' there means updating documents, not the controlling a stage workshop. Benefits are mostly confirmed after closure, so post-project reviews must be planned.

items: Stage boundary: review the stage, approve the updated release map, confirm justification and risks.
Release planning workshop: introduction, OKR definition, release planning, wrap-up.
Closing: prepare closure, confirm acceptance, evaluate, request closure; the board authorizes.
Closure workshop: final demo, project lessons, progress review, lessons report, handover planning.
Closing sits in the final stage; benefits reviews continue after it.

summary: You can now run a stage boundary around the release planning workshop, from OKRs to an updated release map. You can also close a project through the right activities and closure workshop topics, and know what the board checks before it authorizes closure.

A.q: Saltmarsh Housing Group's Repairs Reimagined project is at the end of stage 2. In the release planning workshop, the service design team sets the objective 'tenants trust that repairs are fixed first time' with the key result 'second visits below 20% on the pilot estate'. Which topic is this?
A.why: OKR definition defines or updates team OKRs, linking aspirational objectives to measurable key results (Table 13.16, 12.3.2.3).

whyNot.0: Release planning breaks key activities into user stories and updates the release map.
whyNot.1: The introduction presents the canvas, project backlog and release map and gathers feedback.
whyNot.3: Wrap-up reviews the key outputs of the workshop; it does not define the measures of progress.

A.q: Larkspur Rail's Fair Fares project is closing. In the project closure workshop, small groups bring the PID, project logs, project dashboard and Agilometer up to date so that the records are complete for the move to operations. Which topic is this?
A.why: The closure workshop's progress review topic updates all project documentation, including the PID, logs, project dashboard and Agilometer (Table 13.19).

whyNot.1: The lessons report topic defines actionable lessons for future projects.
whyNot.2: Final handover planning sets support responsibilities, operational needs and benefits actions.
whyNot.3: Project lessons presents lessons gathered from the project's phases and team members.

A.q: Callowmere University's Student Support Hub is closing. Jamal Hussain prepares follow-on recommendations for the unbuilt early-warning feature and open risks, checks that the benefits management approach includes post-project benefit reviews, and confirms from the PID how the hub passes to operations. Which activity is this?
A.why: Confirming project acceptance includes follow-on action recommendations for unfinished work, issues and risks, checking post-project benefits activities and confirming delivery to operations (Table 13.18).

whyNot.0: Evaluating the project compares results with the original PID and produces the end project and lessons reports.
whyNot.2: Authorizing project closure is the board's decision in directing, not the PM's preparation of follow-on actions.
whyNot.3: Requesting closure briefs the board on performance and readiness and asks it to close the project.

B.q: Pinewick Home and Garden's project is at the end of stage 2. Patrick Dunne, with the project team, reviews and updates parts of the PID, picks out lessons from the stock-level release to apply next, and adds the stage 3 details to the release map. Which activity is this?
options: Authorize a stage or exception plan
B.why: Preparing the next stage plan reviews and updates PID components, reviews lessons for the next stage and updates the release map with the next stage's details (Table 13.15).

whyNot.0: Evaluating stage status is a controlling a stage activity that reviews progress during the stage.
whyNot.1: Preparing the project plan happens in initiation, where the project-level release map is documented.
whyNot.2: Authorizing a stage plan is the board's decision in directing, after the PM has prepared it.

B.q: Easterholm County Council's Care Online project is closing. In the project closure workshop, the team drafts a plan setting out which support tasks the social care operations team will take on, what it needs to run the service and which benefits actions follow. Which topic is this?
B.why: Final handover planning develops a hand-over plan with support responsibilities, operational requirements and benefits management actions (Table 13.19).

whyNot.1: The final product demo shows the finished product for user acceptance.
whyNot.2: The lessons report sets actionable lessons for future projects.
whyNot.3: The progress review updates the PID, logs, project dashboard and Agilometer.

B.q: Draycott Precision Engineering's project closure workshop reaches a topic where the group turns what it has learned into actions for future projects, adding the trends from its Agilometer and psychological safety assessments. Which topic is this?
B.why: The lessons report topic defines actionable lessons for future projects, including Agilometer and psychological safety trends where possible (Table 13.19).

whyNot.0: Project lessons presents the lessons gathered; turning them into actions for future projects is the lessons report.
whyNot.1: The progress review brings the documentation up to date for transition.
whyNot.3: The final product demo confirms the product meets requirements and is ready for hand-over.

C.q: Larkspur Rail's Fair Fares project is at the end of stage 3. The board proposes skipping the release planning workshop because each team already plans its sprints in team planning workshops. Is this an appropriate application of the 'managing a stage boundary' process, and why?
options: Yes, because each team plans its iterations in team planning
Yes, because the board approves the release map in directing
No, because the workshop plans the next stage's release map
No, because the board should write the teams' OKRs itself
C.why: The release planning workshop aligns the teams with the vision and plans the next stage together, setting OKRs and updating the release map that the board will approve (13.7.4.1, Table 13.16).

whyNot.0: Team planning covers the next iteration only; it does not produce the stage-level release map.
whyNot.1: The board does approve the release map, but it needs the workshop to prepare it.
whyNot.3: The verdict is right but the reason is wrong: teams define or update their own OKRs in the workshop.

C.q: Callowmere University's project is closing. Because Release 1 already shows high booking numbers, the board authorizes closure without arranging any post-project benefits reviews. Is this an appropriate application of the 'directing a project' process, and why?
options: Yes, because benefits can be realized during the project
Yes, because the end project report confirms the benefits
No, because benefits must be confirmed before the last release
No, because the board should ensure post-project benefits reviews
C.why: In 'authorize project closure' the board ensures post-project benefits reviews cover the product in operational use; benefits are mostly confirmed after closure (Table 13.4, 6.3.1).

whyNot.0: Some benefits can be realized during the project, but most are confirmed after closure, so reviews are still needed.
whyNot.1: The end project report reviews performance against the PID; it does not replace benefits reviews after closure.
whyNot.2: The verdict is right but the reason is wrong: confirming benefits mostly happens after the project closes.

C.q: Saltmarsh Housing Group's project is in its final stage. Sally Greaves holds the project closure workshop at month 12 and opens it with a demo of the finished service to the tenants' panel, collecting their final feedback and acceptance. Is this an appropriate application of the 'closing a project' process, and why?
options: Yes, because closing is a separate stage after delivery
Yes, because the final demo confirms readiness for hand-over
No, because acceptance belongs in the progress review workshop
No, because tenants on the panel do not hold a project role
C.why: The final product demo topic demonstrates the product for user acceptance and gathers final feedback, confirming it meets requirements and is ready for hand-over (Table 13.19).

whyNot.0: Closing happens within the final stage; it is not a separate stage.
whyNot.2: Progress reviews include demos during stages, but final acceptance before hand-over is a closure workshop topic.
whyNot.3: Users giving acceptance do not need a project role; the panel represents the tenants who will use the service.

reteach.title: A long sailing voyage in legs
reteach.question: When a yacht reaches each harbour, what does the crew decide before the next leg, and what happens when the voyage ends?

blocks.h: Harbour stops and the final mooring
blocks.body: At each harbour the skipper reviews the leg just sailed, the crew agrees goals for the next leg and marks the route on the chart, and the owner approves it. That is a stage boundary with its release planning workshop. At the final port, the crew shows the owner the boat, shares lessons, updates the log, writes advice for future voyages and hands the boat to the marina team.

items.label: Review leg, update chart: next stage plan

blocks.text: Planning each day's watches is not the harbour meeting. Release planning sets the next stage; team planning sets the next iteration.

explain.body: Managing a stage boundary lets the PM give the board enough to review the current stage, review the updated release map, approve the next stage plan and confirm the business justification and risks are still acceptable.

test.q: Easterholm County Council's Release 1 is live. The board now wants to know whether stage 2 succeeded, see the updated release map, approve the plan for stage 3 and confirm the project is still justified. Which process provides this?
test.why: Managing a stage boundary gives the board what it needs to review the stage, approve the next stage plan and confirm justification and risks (13.7.1).

whyNot.0: Controlling a stage manages day-to-day work within a stage, not the decision to move to the next.
whyNot.1: Initiating builds the project's foundations before it is authorized.
whyNot.2: Managing product delivery controls the link between the PM and a delivery team for work packages.

explain.body: In the release planning workshop, the 'release planning' topic breaks key activities into user stories and updates the release map with more detail on the next stage or release.

test.q: In Pinewick Home and Garden's release planning workshop for stage 4, the teams break the roll-out to all 85 stores into user stories and update the release map with more detail on Release 3. Which topic is this?
test.why: The release planning topic breaks key activities into user stories and updates the release map with the next stage's detail (Table 13.16).

whyNot.1: OKR definition sets objectives and key results for the teams.
whyNot.2: The introduction presents the canvas, project backlog and release map for feedback.
whyNot.3: Wrap-up reviews the key outputs of the workshop rather than adding detail to the release map.

explain.body: The PM reviews the original intent in the PID and the approved changes, prepares the end project report, and reviews the project log for lessons to include in the lessons report.

test.q: Draycott Precision Engineering's project is closing. Andrea Lucas compares what was delivered with the original PID and approved changes, writes the end project report, and draws lessons from the project log into a lessons report. Which activity is this?
test.why: Evaluating the project reviews the original PID and approved changes, prepares the end project report and the lessons report (Table 13.18).

whyNot.0: Confirming acceptance covers follow-on actions, benefits checks and hand-over to operations.
whyNot.1: Requesting closure briefs the board and asks it to close the project.
whyNot.3: Preparing planned closure updates the log and release map with actuals and drafts the closure notification.

explain.body: In 'authorize project closure' the board reviews the original and current PID, approves the end project report, ensures post-project benefits reviews cover the product in operational use and confirms the updated project canvas.

test.q: Larkspur Rail's project manager has asked to close Fair Fares. The board compares the original and current PID, approves the end project report, makes sure benefits reviews are planned after go-live and confirms the updated canvas. Which activity is the board performing?
test.why: Authorizing project closure is the board's directing activity covering these checks (Table 13.4).

whyNot.0: Requesting closure is the PM's last closing activity, before the board decides.
whyNot.2: Confirming acceptance is a PM activity in closing a project.
whyNot.3: Evaluating the project is the PM's review that produces the end project report the board then approves.
